All rates are derived from the formulas (raw rate \(= SF \cdot B / M\), before preamble and FEC), not measured. Before this change CSS sent one bit per 20 ms chirp (50 bit/s) whatever sf was set to; see the SF table for every SF at 2 and 4 kHz.

Note that the lower part of a 17–21 kHz band is audible to many people.

docs.title: OFDM mode
docs.text:
Implementation (derived from code). sw_ofdm_modulate builds a real-valued OFDM signal with an \(N\)-point IFFT and Hermitian symmetry. Data and pilot subcarriers are placed only inside the configured band \([f_c - B/2,\ f_c + B/2]\) (carrier_freq ± bandwidth/2; default 19 kHz ± 1 kHz = 18–20 kHz). See Mathematical model §2.2.3.

  • Subcarrier spacing: \(\Delta f = f_s / N\).
  • Active bins \(k_{lo} = \lceil (f_c - B/2) N / f_s \rceil + 1\) to \(k_{hi} = \lfloor (f_c + B/2) N / f_s \rfloor - 1\): one empty guard bin inside each band edge. DC, the audible range, the Nyquist bin and their mirrors stay empty on TX and RX.
  • Rejected configurations (SW_ERR_BAD_PARAM): band reaching DC, band edge closer than \(\Delta f\) to Nyquist, fewer than 4 active bins.
  • Every 8th active bin (starting with the first) is a pilot (+1, −1, …). The rest carry BPSK (1 bit) or QPSK (2 bits). Data bits are whitened with PRBS15 so repeated payload bytes never produce identical symbols. Pilots track the common phase of each data symbol.
  • Preamble: two identical Zadoff-Chu OFDM symbols (root 1) on the active bins, joined phase-continuously. They are used for timing (Schmidl-Cox, then phase-slope fine timing), CFO, the channel estimate and the noise estimate.
  • Each symbol has a cyclic prefix of cp_length samples (C default \(N/8\) when 0; the app and CLI default is 64). Its first \(\lfloor N_{cp}/2\rfloor\) samples carry a raised-cosine cross-fade with the previous symbol; the frame ends with a \(\lfloor N_{cp}/2\rfloor\)-sample fade-out.

CP) Raw rate BPSK / QPSK Max app frame (255 B, QPSK) 256 / 64, 18–20 kHz (default) 172.3 Hz 10 / 2 / 8 18.26–19.81 kHz 320 samples (7.26 ms) 1.10 / 2.21 kbit/s 944 ms 256 / 32, 18–20 kHz 172.3 Hz 10 / 2 / 8 18.26–19.81 kHz 288 (6.53 ms) 1.23 / 2.45 kbit/s 849 ms 512 / 64, 18–20 kHz 86.1 Hz 22 / 3 / 19 18.09–19.90 kHz 576 (13.06 ms) 1.45 / 2.91 kbit/s 732 ms 1024 / 128, 18–20 kHz 43.1 Hz 45 / 6 / 39 18.04–19.94 kHz 1152 (26.12 ms) 1.49 / 2.99 kbit/s 759 ms 2048 / 128, 18–20 kHz 21.5 Hz 91 / 12 / 79 18.02–19.96 kHz 2176 (49.34 ms) 1.60 / 3.20 kbit/s 742 ms 2048 / 128, 18–21 kHz (High Speed preset) 21.5 Hz 138 / 18 / 120 18.02–20.97 kHz 2176 (49.34 ms) 2.43 / 4.86 kbit/s 544 ms

The ~1 % outside the band is the main lobe of the outermost subcarriers, within a few hundred hertz of the band edges.

Before this change the OFDM modulator ignored carrier_freq and bandwidth and spread energy over 5.7–21.9 kHz (N = 256): only about 11–15 % of the energy fell in 18–20 kHz and about −2 dB (≈ 60 %) was below 16 kHz (pure-Python model of the old modulator, same frame; peak samples 7–19).

The raw IDFT peaks above exceed full scale (and did more before the last symbol's zero padding was whitened, see data whitening); across the configurations in test_tx_peak they reach about 2–6 with crest factors of 9–19 dB. The modulator therefore normalises every frame to a peak of exactly amplitude (default 0.8) with one gain per frame (see Transmit level in the mathematical model); the energy fractions above do not depend on the level. The app and soundwave-cli play or write the samples unscaled, and native/tests/test_tx_peak.c checks max |sample| ≤ amplitude across FFT sizes, CP lengths, BPSK/QPSK, bands and worst-case payloads.

Not measured over the air

The band plan and spectrum are exact properties of the transmitted samples. Whether a given speaker and microphone pass 18–20 kHz, and what SNR they achieve there, has not been measured; see the field test plan. Many devices roll off above 18–20 kHz, which is why the default band stops at 20 kHz.

docs.title: Receiver chain (both modes)
docs.text:
1. AGC (optional, app default on): target RMS 0.25, attack 1 ms, release 100 ms, gain range −20 to +32 dB (math §6).
  2. Frame detection (sw_detect_frame): CSS converts to complex baseband and scores every lag on all 10 preamble chirps with normalised up-/down-chirp correlations over the whole buffer; the first preamble wins, and the up/down peak split gives fractional timing and the frequency offset (math §3.1). OFDM uses the Schmidl-Cox metric on the repeated ZC preamble as presence gate, then the earliest strong peak of a normalised matched filter on the known preamble, refined from the preamble's phase slope.
  3. CFO: Schmidl-Cox on the two repeated preamble symbols (OFDM), computed on the analytic signal.
  4. CSS: dechirp each symbol at the chip rate and take the \(2^{SF}\)-point FFT peak (Gray demapping). OFDM: the FFT window backs off \(\lfloor N_{cp}/4\rfloor\) samples into the CP (after the transmit cross-fade). Then a least-squares channel estimate from the preamble, a noise-variance estimate, per-symbol pilot phase correction, ZF or MMSE equalization, and de-whitening.
  5. Demapping to bits, then in the app FrameCodec.decode: RS(255,223) decoding (up to 16 byte errors) and CRC-32 verification.

docs.title: Contributing to Soundwave
docs.text: First off, thank you for considering contributing to Soundwave! Soundwave is an open-source ultrasonic physical layer (PHY) library bringing cross-platform acoustic data transmission to desktop, mobile, and web applications.

docs.title: Code of Conduct & Contribution Philosophy
docs.text:
• Authenticity & Excellence: Write clean, self-documented, high-performance C11 and Dart code.
  • No Masking of Symptoms: Never bypass failed assertions or swallow exceptions silently. Fix underlying root causes.
  • Empirical Verification: Always run native tests (ctest) and Flutter unit tests before submitting a Pull Request.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text: This page covers the native C core, the soundwave-cli tool, the Flutter app on each platform, and the documentation site. The commands match the CI workflows (.github/workflows/ci.yml, build.yml, release.yml, docs.yml). If this page and a workflow disagree, the workflow is what CI actually runs.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Component Requirement Used by CI Native core CMake ≥ 3.20, a C11 compiler (GCC, Clang, AppleClang or MSVC) and a C++ compiler (only for the Catch2 test runner) ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest Flutter app Flutter 3.47.x stable (macOS release jobs pin 3.50.0, see CI/CD) subosito/flutter-action@v2 Android Android SDK + NDK + CMake 3.22+ (Gradle installs them on demand), JDK 17 build.yml → build-android Linux desktop GTK 3 development headers and the usual Flutter Linux dependencies (clang, ninja-build, pkg-config, libgtk-3-dev) build.yml Docs site Python 3.10+, pip install -r docs/requirements.txt; optionally Doxygen and the Flutter SDK for the API pages docs.yml

All third-party C code is vendored in native/vendor/ (KissFFT, miniaudio), so there are no submodules to fetch.

docs.title: 1. Native core and tests
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/PxA-Labs/ultrasonic-phy-layer.git
cd ultrasonic-phy-layer/native
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --config Release --parallel
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure --build-config Release

This builds libsoundwave (static and shared), the test executables (test_crc, test_rs_decoder, test_ofdm_demodulate, test_ber, test_e2e, ... and the Catch2 runner catch_tests), the fuzz smoke tests (fuzz_*_smoke), and soundwave-cli.

Useful CMake options (see native/CMakeLists.txt):

Option Default Effect SW_BUILD_TESTS ON Unit/integration tests and CTest registration SW_BUILD_BENCHMARKS OFF Micro-benchmarks in native/benchmarks/ SW_BUILD_COVERAGE OFF gcov/lcov instrumentation SW_ENABLE_ASAN / SW_ENABLE_UBSAN OFF Sanitizers SW_ENABLE_FUZZER OFF libFuzzer harnesses (LLVM Clang) SW_FUZZ_SMOKE ON Fuzz harnesses as CTest smoke tests

Presets are available too: cmake --preset release (also default, debug, asan, ubsan, fuzz). Sanitizers and fuzzing are covered in the developer guide.

docs.title: 2. soundwave-cli
docs.text:
soundwave-cli is built with the core on every host platform (it is skipped for Android):

cmake --build native/build --target soundwave_cli
./native/build/soundwave-cli modulate --mode css --input "Hello" --output hello.wav
./native/build/soundwave-cli demodulate --mode css --input hello.wav

See the CLI guide.

docs.title: 3. Flutter app
docs.text:
The app loads libsoundwave at run time through dart:ffi. How the library gets next to the app depends on the platform.

LinuxWindowsmacOSAndroid 
cd soundwave_app
flutter pub get
flutter run -d linux            # debug
flutter build linux --release   # bundle in build/linux/x64/release/bundle/

soundwave_app/linux/CMakeLists.txt builds native/ as an ExternalProject and installs libsoundwave.so into bundle/lib/. Packaging (.tar.gz, .deb, AppImage) is done by soundwave_app/linux/packaging/package.sh.

cd soundwave_app
flutter pub get
flutter run -d windows
flutter build windows --release

soundwave_app/windows/CMakeLists.txt builds native/ and copies it next to soundwave.exe as soundwave.dll. windows/packaging/package.ps1 creates the zip and MSIX.

cd soundwave_app
flutter pub get
flutter build macos --release
./macos/packaging/embed_native.sh   # builds a universal libsoundwave.dylib into Contents/Frameworks

For flutter run -d macos during development, build the library first (cmake -S native -B native/build && cmake --build native/build --target soundwave_shared). The app also searches ../native/build/.

cd soundwave_app
flutter build apk --debug
flutter build apk --release --split-per-abi
flutter build appbundle --release

Gradle's externalNativeBuild compiles native/CMakeLists.txt with the NDK for arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a and x86_64. Audio uses miniaudio's AAudio backend (API 26+) with an OpenSL ES fallback. Release signing reads android/key.properties; without it, release builds are debug-signed. Details are in the developer guide.

iOS is not set up: there is no ios/ directory.

docs.title: Running the Flutter tests
docs.text:
cmake -S native -B native/build-ffi -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DSW_BUILD_TESTS=OFF
cmake --build native/build-ffi --target soundwave_shared
cd soundwave_app
SOUNDWAVE_LIB=$PWD/../native/build-ffi/libsoundwave.so flutter test

Without a loadable library, the real-DSP loopback tests in test/native/ are skipped. CI sets SOUNDWAVE_REQUIRE_NATIVE=1 so that a missing library fails the run instead.

docs.text:
pip install -r docs/requirements.txt

(cd soundwave_app && flutter pub get && dart doc --output ../docs/api/dart .)   # optional: Dart API HTML

docs.title: Using the app
docs.text: The Soundwave app has three tabs: Dashboard, Monitor and Settings. This page walks through a first transfer and then describes each feature as it exists in the code today.

docs.title: First message (two devices)
docs.text:
1. Install and open the app on two devices (see Build from source). On first launch, a five-page tutorial explains the modes and asks for microphone access. You can replay it from Settings → Show tutorial.
  2. Keep the default settings on both devices: CSS mode, 19 kHz centre frequency, 2 kHz sweep, spreading factor 8. Both devices must use the same modem settings.
  3. On the receiver, open Dashboard → Receiver Control → Start Listening.
  4. On the transmitter, type a short message under Transmission Control and tap Send / Modulate & Play. Set the media volume to a moderate level.
  5. Received messages appear under Received Messages Log, together with an estimated SNR.

Expect slow CSS frames

In the default CSS configuration (SF 8, 2 kHz) one 128 ms chirp carries 8 bits, so the raw rate is 62.6 bit/s and a two-byte message takes about 6 s on air. A lower SF or a 4 kHz sweep is faster (SF 6 at 4 kHz: 376 bit/s, about 1 s) but less robust (values computed from the code, see Signal chain). OFDM is much faster (about 2.2 kbit/s raw with the defaults, 4.9 kbit/s with High Speed) and stays in the configured band, 18–20 kHz by default; the OFDM card in Settings shows the computed band and rate.

Start with the devices close together (tens of centimetres) and increase the distance from there. Range has not been measured yet.

docs.text:
An in-browser simulation of the two Soundwave waveforms, generated with the same formulas as the C modulators (css_modulate.c, ofdm_modulate.c). docs.title: CSS: chirp frame
docs.text:
Each chirp carries SF bits. Symbol k (0 ≤ k < M = 2SF) is the base up-chirp started k chips into its sweep: its frequency starts at fc − B/2 + kB/M, rises at B/T and wraps from fc + B/2 to fc − B/2. B = fs/D with D = round(fs/bandwidth) samples per chip, T = M/B. Bits are Gray mapped. A frame starts with 8 base up-chirps and 2 down-chirps. Raw rate = SF·B/M bit/s.

docs.title: OFDM: constellation and band occupancy
docs.text:
Active bins k = N/8+1 … N/2−1 of an N-point IFFT, with Hermitian symmetry so the output is real. Every 8th active bin is a pilot. Data bins carry BPSK (0 → −1, 1 → +1) or QPSK ((±1±j)/√2). x[n] = (1/√N)·Re Σ Xk ej2πkn/N, followed by a cyclic prefix. The constellation adds complex AWGN at the chosen Es/N0 directly on the subcarriers (a perfectly equalized flat channel). The theory curve is Q(√(2Eb/N0)).

docs.title: Full description (≤ 4000 characters)
docs.text:
Soundwave sends data through the air as sound. Type a message or pick a small file, and Soundwave plays it as a high-frequency signal through your speaker. A nearby phone or computer running Soundwave picks it up with its microphone and decodes it. No internet, Bluetooth, pairing or account is needed.

Two modulation modes • CSS (chirp spread spectrum): slow but robust. Each frequency sweep carries 6–10 bits, in the 18–20 kHz range with the default settings. • OFDM: much faster, using many subcarriers at once. In the current version its signal is clearly audible. • Presets for a robust long-range setup and a high-speed OFDM setup, plus full manual control of frequency, sweep, spreading factor, FFT size, cyclic prefix and equalizer.

Built-in error protection Every frame carries a CRC-32 checksum and optional Reed-Solomon error correction. Longer messages and files are split into fragments and reassembled, with optional automatic retransmission (ARQ) when both devices enable it.

See the signal Live spectrum analyzer, waterfall spectrogram, waveform view and OFDM constellation diagram, with an estimated SNR for every received message.

Record, import and export Record what the microphone hears as WAV, import WAV/PCM files and decode them offline, save signal samples, and export your message log as JSON, CSV or TXT.

Private by design No accounts, no ads, no analytics and no crash reporting, and the app does not connect to the internet. Audio is processed on your device and nothing leaves it unless you share it. Note that transmissions are broadcast as sound and are not encrypted: anyone nearby with a compatible receiver can hear them, so do not send sensitive information.

Good to know • Range and speed depend heavily on your speaker, microphone, volume and room. Start with the devices close together. • Most adults hear little of the CSS band, but children and pets may. • Soundwave is experimental, open-source software (Apache 2.0): github.com/PxA-Labs/ultrasonic-phy-layer

docs.title: Field Test Plan: BER/FER vs Distance, Multipath and Doppler
docs.text: Covers issue #96. No field results exist yet. This document is the procedure. Results go into docs/BER_FIELD_TEST_RESULTS.md, which should be created only once real measurements have been made (template in §9).

docs.title: 1. Objectives and acceptance criteria
docs.text:
# Question PRD target How it is decided O1 Error rate at the reference SNR BER < 10⁻⁵ at 10 dB SNR (CSS and OFDM) §6.4 statistics; definitions in §2 O2 Usable range ≥ 5 m in at least one environment FER ≤ 1 % (proposed) at the distance, CSS default config O3 Multipath robustness (none) FER per environment at 1 m and 3 m O4 Doppler tolerance (none) FER at ±1 m/s compared with the static result at the same distance O5 Stability (none) FER drift over 1 h, interference cases

Two definitions the team must agree on before testing

  1. "BER" in the PRD. soundwave-cli only reports frames that pass RS + CRC-32, so post-FEC residual BER is effectively always 0. The measurable quantities are FER (frame error rate), residual BER on delivered frames, and RS symbols corrected (a lower bound on the pre-FEC byte error rate). Proposal: judge O1 by residual BER including lost frames. Count every lost frame as a failure, and require 0 lost frames and 0 bit errors over ≥ 3 × 10⁵ payload bits (95 % confidence that BER < 10⁻⁵, rule of three). Measuring raw channel BER would need a new CLI option that dumps pre-FEC bits; that option does not exist.
  2. "SNR". The CLI prints an SNR estimate from preamble detection (sw_detect_frame). It is uncalibrated and its definition is specific to the implementation. Record it, but also record the acoustic quantities (signal SPL and noise floor at the receiver, §5.3). Do not report a "10 dB SNR" point unless it was measured with a stated method.

docs.title: 2. Metrics
docs.text: Metric Definition Source FER frames not delivered ÷ frames sent ber_sweep.py decode → summary.json Residual BER bit errors in delivered payloads ÷ delivered payload bits (95 % upper bound 3/n when 0 errors) same RS correction rate RS symbols corrected ÷ (delivered frames × codeword bytes) same CLI SNR estimate median of snr = … dB printed by soundwave-cli demodulate same Signal level SPL at the receiver microphone position during a frame, dB(Z) Sound level meter Noise floor SPL with the transmitter silent, dB(Z), plus a 30 s WAV recording Sound level meter + recording Delay spread (optional) RT60 of the room as a proxy (§5.4) RT60 app/meter

docs.title: 3. Two test pipelines
docs.text:
The app and soundwave-cli use the same frame format and modem defaults (see Architecture), so a recording from either pipeline can be decoded by either tool as long as the settings match.

Pipeline A: CLI playback, offline decode (primary) Pipeline B: app to app (end-to-end check) TX Any device plays playlist.wav from ber_sweep.py generate (media player, or a laptop with a speaker) Soundwave app, Send RX Any recorder at 44.1 kHz, 16-bit or 32-bit float, mono or stereo, with audio processing off (or the app's Record button, which records unprocessed through miniaudio) Soundwave app, listening Decode ber_sweep.py decode (wraps soundwave-cli demodulate) Live, in the app Output Per-frame CSV + summary JSON Exported message log (JSON) with SNR per message Strength Repeatable: the same recording can be re-decoded after DSP changes Exercises the real app stack, AGC and link layer

Phone voice-memo apps often apply AGC, noise suppression and low-pass filtering that remove the 17–22 kHz band. Use a recorder with an "unprocessed" or "raw" mode, or the Soundwave app's own recorder.

Many meters roll off above 12.5 kHz, so record the meter model and its rated range Tape measure, 2 stands/tripods Devices at 1.0 m height, centre to centre Repeatable geometry Protractor or angle template 0°, 45°, 90°, 180° Speaker and mic directivity Thermometer / hygrometer ±1 °C, ±5 % RH Air absorption at ultrasonic frequencies depends on both (ISO 9613-1) Laptop with soundwave-cli and Python 3 Built from the same commit as the app Generate and decode Doppler rig (optional) Trolley or slider on a ≥ 4 m straight track, a metronome, a stopwatch or video at ≥ 60 fps 1 m/s motion Interference sources Bluetooth speaker with a fixed music track and a speech track Stress tests

docs.title: 5.1 Build and generate the test signals
docs.text:
cmake -S native -B native/build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DSW_BUILD_TESTS=OFF
cmake --build native/build --target soundwave_cli
export SOUNDWAVE_CLI=$PWD/native/build/soundwave-cli

# CSS default config (SF 8, 2 kHz): 20 frames x 64 B (~14.3 s/frame), 1 s gaps
python3 docs/testing/ber_sweep.py generate --mode css --frames 20 --payload-bytes 64 \
  --gap 1.0 --lead-in 2.0 --verify --out runs/css64
# OFDM default config (N=256, CP=64, QPSK, ZF): 200 frames x 64 B, 0.3 s gaps
python3 docs/testing/ber_sweep.py generate --mode ofdm --frames 200 --payload-bytes 64 \
  --gap 0.3 --lead-in 2.0 --verify --out runs/ofdm64
# Offline baseline (SIMULATED, AWGN): run before going into the field
python3 docs/testing/ber_sweep.py simulate --manifest runs/css64/manifest.json --snr 0,3,6,10,20

--verify decodes every clean frame once, so a broken build is caught before any field time is spent. Keep manifest.json with the recordings, because decoding needs it.

docs.title: 5.2 Transmit level
docs.text:
1. Put the sound level meter at 1.0 m on the transmitter axis.
  2. Play playlist.wav (or send a long CSS message from the app) and read the maximum level, dB(Z), during a frame.
  3. Adjust the device volume until it reads ≤ 80 dB(Z) SPL at 1 m (PRD compliance limit). Record the volume step and the reading.
  4. Never exceed this level, and never hold a transmitting device near anyone's ears.

docs.title: 5.3 Noise floor and signal level at the receiver
docs.text:
At every test position:

  1. Measure SPL with the transmitter silent for 30 s (LZeq), and record 30 s of WAV on the receiver.
  2. Measure SPL during a frame.
  3. Write down temperature and relative humidity.

docs.title: 5.4 Room characterization (multipath)
docs.text: The repo has no impulse-response tool. As a proxy, measure RT60 (any room-acoustics app or meter that uses interrupted noise or impulse methods) and describe the surfaces. Each recording of playlist.wav is saved, so a delay-spread analysis can be added later without repeating the measurement.

docs.title: 6.1 Configurations
docs.text:
ID Mode Parameters Raw rate (derived) C1 CSS f_c 19 kHz, B 2 kHz, SF 8 (default) 62.6 bit/s C2 CSS f_c 18 kHz, B 2 kHz, SF 10 (Long Range preset) 19.6 bit/s O1 OFDM N 256, CP 64, QPSK, ZF, 18–20 kHz (default) 2.2 kbit/s O2 OFDM N 256, CP 64, QPSK, MMSE, 18–20 kHz 2.2 kbit/s O3 OFDM N 256, CP 64, BPSK, MMSE, 18–20 kHz 1.1 kbit/s

docs.title: 6.2 Distance (line of sight, 0°, devices at 1.0 m height)
docs.text: Environment Distances (m) Configs E1: quietest available room (furnished bedroom or studio) 0.5, 1, 2, 3 C1, O1, O2 E2: office (normal HVAC, no speech) 1, 3, 5 C1, C2, O1, O2 E3: large room or hall 1, 3, 5, 8 C1, C2, O1

docs.title: 6.3 Angle, multipath and Doppler
docs.text:
Test Positions Configs Angle 1 m and 3 m at 0°, 45°, 90°, 180° (receiver behind the transmitter) C1, O1 Reverberant room (kitchen/bathroom, hard surfaces) 1 m, 3 m C1, O1, O2 Corner (TX facing a corner 0.5 m away, RX 2 m behind) fixed C1, O1 Absorptive room (soft furnishings) 1 m, 3 m C1, O1 Doppler: TX moving at 1 m/s toward the RX, from 4 m to 1 m 5 runs C1, O1 Doppler: TX moving at 1 m/s away, from 1 m to 4 m 5 runs C1, O1

At 1 m/s a 4 m track gives 3 s of motion per pass. That covers OFDM frames (≈ 50 ms each) but not one CSS frame (≈ 14.3 s at 64 B). For CSS, use 12 B payloads (≈ 7.7 s/frame, still longer than one pass) and treat the CSS Doppler result as qualitative only, or run a back-and-forth track for the full frame and log the motion profile. Expect CSS to fail here: 1 m/s is a ≈ 55 Hz shift at 19 kHz, about 7 FFT bins at SF 8 / 2 kHz, while the receiver removes only a static offset of up to about ±2 bins measured on the preamble (derived, see Mathematical model §3.1).

docs.title: 6.4 How many frames (statistics)
docs.text:
Goal Required observation 64 B payload frames CSS C1 airtime OFDM O1 airtime Screening FER to about ±10 % 20 frames 20 ≈ 5 min ≈ 7 s "10,000-bit sequence" (issue #96) 10,000 payload bits 20 ≈ 5 min ≈ 7 s Residual BER < 10⁻⁵ at 95 % confidence (O1) 3 × 10⁵ error-free payload bits, 0 lost frames 586 ≈ 2.5 h ≈ 3.4 min

Airtime is derived from the code and includes the generator's gaps (1 s for CSS, 0.3 s for OFDM). A 10,000-bit run can only support a residual-BER claim down to about 3 × 10⁻⁴. Run the full O1 sample only at the reference point (E2, 3 m), and use 20-frame screening runs everywhere else.

docs.text: Test Procedure Config Long run 1 h continuous playlist at E2, 3 m. Log device temperature at start and end O1 (and C1 if time allows) Music Bluetooth speaker 1 m from the RX playing the fixed music track at 60 and 70 dB(Z) at the RX position C1, O1 Speech Same, with the speech track C1, O1 Second ultrasonic source A second transmitter 2 m away playing a different playlist at the same level, starting at random times C1, O1

docs.title: 7. Procedure for one test point (pipeline A)
docs.text:
1. Place the devices, measure the distance and angle, and photograph the setup.
  2. Record the environment data and the noise floor (§5.3).
  3. Start recording on the receiver (44.1 kHz).
  4. Play playlist.wav on the transmitter at the calibrated volume.
  5. Stop recording 2 s after the playlist ends. Name the file <testid>_<config>_<env>_<dist>m_<angle>deg_<rxdevice>.wav, for example T014_O1_E2_3m_0deg_pixel7.wav.
  6. Decode:
python3 docs/testing/ber_sweep.py decode --manifest runs/ofdm64/manifest.json \
  --recording T014_O1_E2_3m_0deg_pixel7.wav --label T014 --out results/T014
  1. Copy the summary.json values into the results table (§9). Archive the WAV, frames.csv and summary.json.

For pipeline B, send a fixed list of 20 numbered messages (T014-01 … T014-20) from the app, export the receiver's message log as JSON, and count the messages received. FER = missing ÷ 20. SNR comes from the log.

docs.title: 8. Recording conditions to log for every point
docs.text: Test ID, date and time, operator, TX device (model, OS, volume step), RX device (model, OS, recorder app and its processing setting), app/CLI git SHA, config ID, environment ID and description, distance, angle, height, temperature, RH, noise floor dB(Z), signal dB(Z), RT60 (if measured), frames sent and delivered, FER, residual bit errors, payload bits, RS corrections, median CLI SNR, and notes.

docs.title: 9. Recording results
docs.text:
Create docs/BER_FIELD_TEST_RESULTS.md only when data exists, with:

  1. The environment and equipment list (models, meter class and frequency range).
  2. One CSV-style table per test group, with the columns from §8.
  3. Plots (FER vs distance per config). Generate them from the CSVs and commit the script that made them.
  4. A PASS/FAIL table against §1. Every number must point to an archived recording or result file.
  5. A Limitations section (device count, meter bandwidth, SNR definition).

Never mix simulated (ber_sweep.py simulate, CI) numbers into these tables. If they are shown for comparison, label them SIMULATED.

docs.title: 10. Safety
docs.text: Keep the transmit level ≤ 80 dB(Z) at 1 m. Tell people in the area before testing, keep pets out of the test room, and stop if anyone reports discomfort. OFDM mode is clearly audible on the current build.

docs.title: Hardware Profiling Plan: Latency, Startup, Memory, CPU
docs.text: Covers issue #98. No measurements exist yet. This page describes how to make them. Results go into docs/PERFORMANCE_BENCHMARKS.md, which should be created only once real data exists (see §8).

docs.title: 1. Targets (from the PRD) and how each is defined here
docs.text:
Metric PRD target Operational definition used in this plan Audio latency < 50 ms capture-to-output (a) The device audio path round trip, measured with a loopback tool. (b) Soundwave processing latency: time from the end of a frame's audio at the receiver microphone to the message appearing on screen. See §3 Startup < 2 s cold launch Time to the first rendered frame after a cold start (process not running) Memory < 120 MB RAM Peak PSS (Android) or resident/working set (desktop) of the app process, with the Dart heap and native heap reported separately CPU < 15 % on a mid-range device Mean process CPU over 60 s, reported both as % of one core and as % of all cores (the PRD does not say which)

Messages take a long time on air (CSS default: about 6 s for even a 2-byte message, derived from the code), so "latency" must never be measured as send-to-receive time without subtracting the airtime.

docs.title: 2. Device and OS matrix
docs.text:
Platform Minimum the build actually supports Devices to test Android minSdk = Flutter SDK default (check aapt dump badging on the APK). AAudio needs API 26+, and older versions use the OpenSL ES fallback One mid-range phone (Pixel 5 class), one low-end phone, one API 26–28 device Windows MSIX MinVersion 10.0.17763 (Windows 10 1809) Windows 10 and Windows 11, x64 macOS MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET 12.0 One Apple Silicon and one Intel Mac (the universal build) Linux Release built on Ubuntu 22.04 (glibc 2.35). Ubuntu 20.04, which issue #98 lists, cannot run these binaries Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04, x64, PulseAudio/PipeWire

Plus three speaker/microphone hardware configurations: built-in, a USB audio interface, and a Bluetooth headset. A Bluetooth headset is expected to fail at ultrasonic frequencies because of codec band limits; record that as a result, not as an error.

Always use release or profile builds. Debug builds use the Dart JIT and are not representative.

docs.title: 3a. Device audio-path round trip (per platform)
docs.text:
Platform Tool / method Android Google OboeTester → Round Trip Latency with a loopback adapter (or acoustically, speaker to mic). Test both the AAudio and OpenSL ES APIs Windows, macOS, Linux A loopback cable from line-out to line-in (or an audio interface). Play an impulse and record it with any tool that timestamps playback and capture on the same clock (for example a DAW's latency measurement, or jack_iodelay on Linux with JACK)

This measures the hardware and OS path that libsoundwave uses through miniaudio. It is not Soundwave-specific.

docs.title: 3b. Soundwave processing latency
docs.text:
The app has no built-in timestamps for this today. Method (no code changes needed):

  1. Put the TX and RX devices side by side and film both screens and the TX speaker with a phone at 240 fps (or ≥ 60 fps).
  2. Send a short message (pipeline B in the field test plan). Record the config.
  3. From the video, measure t₀ (TX Send tap registered, button state change) and t₁ (message visible on RX).
  4. Processing latency ≈ (t₁ − t₀) − frame airtime − TX scheduling time. Take the airtime from Signal chain or FrameGeometry.
  5. Repeat 10 times per config (CSS default, OFDM default).

The video gives no reference for the moment the frame actually ends, so this estimates the upper bound of RX processing to within ±1 video frame plus the uncertainty of the TX start. A more accurate method would add timestamps to RxEngine (frame end sample index → decode completion). That would be a code change, which this plan only recommends.

docs.title: 4. Startup time (cold)
docs.text:
Platform Command / method Android adb shell am force-stop com.pxalabs.soundwave then adb shell am start -W -n com.pxalabs.soundwave/.MainActivity. Record TotalTime (ms). Repeat 10 times and report the median and max. Optionally capture a Perfetto trace All platforms flutter run --profile --trace-startup -d <device> writes build/start_up_info.json (timeToFirstFrameMicros, timeToFrameworkInitMicros). Repeat 5 times Windows/macOS/Linux (release package) Reboot or drop caches (sync; echo 3 \| sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches on Linux) for a true cold start. Measure launch to first window with a 240 fps video of the screen if no trace is available

Report first launch (onboarding shown) and later launches (onboarding skipped) separately.

docs.title: 5. Memory
docs.text:
Platform Command Android adb shell dumpsys meminfo com.pxalabs.soundwave: record TOTAL PSS, Native Heap, Dalvik Heap, Graphics. Sample every 5 s with a loop and keep the peak Windows Get-Process soundwave \| Select-Object WorkingSet64, PrivateMemorySize64, sampled every 5 s macOS footprint -p <pid> or vmmap --summary <pid> (physical footprint) Linux grep -E 'VmRSS\|VmHWM' /proc/<pid>/status (VmHWM is the peak RSS) Dart heap (all) Flutter DevTools → Memory (profile build): peak Dart heap and external memory

Native allocations to keep in mind: one-second capture and playback ring buffers, per-frame modulation buffers, KissFFT plans, and the 10 s rolling sample buffer (≈ 480k samples) used by Save Signal Sample.

docs.title: 6. CPU
docs.text: Platform Command Android adb shell top -H -d 1 -p <pid> (per thread) or adb shell dumpsys cpuinfo. Perfetto for detail Windows Get-Counter '\Process(soundwave)\% Processor Time' -SampleInterval 1 -MaxSamples 60 (the value is % of one core; divide by the core count for % of total) macOS top -pid <pid> -l 60 -s 1 -stats cpu Linux pidstat -u -p <pid> 1 60 (sysstat)

docs.text: ID Scenario Metrics S0 Idle on the Dashboard, not listening Memory, CPU S1 Listening, CSS default, no signal Memory, CPU S2 Listening, CSS default, receiving a frame (TX on another device) Memory peak, CPU S3 Listening, OFDM default, receiving frames every 1 s Memory peak, CPU S4 S3 with the Monitor tab open (spectrum + waterfall + constellation) Memory, CPU, and UI jank (DevTools frame chart) S5 Transmitting a 1 KiB file with ARQ on (OFDM) Memory, CPU S6 WAV recording for 5 min while listening Memory growth (should be flat; the recorder streams to disk) S7 Import and decode a 60 s WAV Peak memory, wall time

docs.title: 8. Recording results
docs.text:
Create docs/PERFORMANCE_BENCHMARKS.md only when data exists. Include:

  • device, OS version, build SHA, build mode, and power state (plugged in, battery saver off);
  • one table per metric: rows are platform × scenario; columns are median, max, number of runs, target, and PASS/FAIL;
  • the raw logs (command output) in an archive or a linked folder;
  • for any FAIL, a linked issue with profiling evidence (trace or DevTools capture).

The DSP micro-benchmarks in native/benchmarks/ (benchmark.yml) measure isolated kernels on CI runners. They are not device measurements and must not be put into these tables.
